question.text: What is Section C of the manual about?

answer.text: Section C of the manual is devoted to safety tips for safe driving and for sharing the road with others.

teaching.text: Asked "What is Section C of the manual devoted to?" a tempting wrong answer is "License fees", but safety tips. Remember: Safety tips section.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Section C of the manual is devoted to safety tips for safe driving and for sharing the road with others.

question.text: Does learning traffic laws end once you have your license?

answer.text: Learning traffic laws and safe habits does not end with your license; drivers are responsible for keeping up with new laws, rules and safety practices for life.

teaching.text: Asked "Who is responsible for keeping up with new traffic laws after you are licensed?" a tempting wrong answer is "Only your driving school", but drivers are responsible for life. Remember: Learning never ends.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Learning traffic laws and safe habits does not end with your license; drivers are responsible for keeping up with new laws, rules and safety practices for life.

question.text: How do new drivers turn the manual's advice into habits?

answer.text: New drivers need practice and experience to turn the manual's written guidance into habits, so the manual advises reviewing it often.

teaching.text: Asked "How do new drivers turn the manual's written guidance into habits?" a tempting wrong answer is "Reading it once", but practice and frequent review. Remember: Practice and review.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New drivers need practice and experience to turn the manual's written guidance into habits, so the manual advises reviewing it often.

question.text: What does aim high in steering mean?

answer.text: Aim high in steering: look as far down the road as you can to pick up the traffic information you need for good decisions.

teaching.text: The aim high in steering rule says to aim high by looking far down the road, while the get the big picture rule says to get the big picture by keeping a proper following distance. Remember: Look far ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Aim high in steering: look as far down the road as you can to pick up the traffic information you need for good decisions.

question.text: How should your eyes work while driving?

answer.text: Keep your eyes moving: scan instead of staring, shifting your gaze constantly so you keep up with changing traffic.

teaching.text: Asked "How should you use your eyes while driving?" a tempting wrong answer is "Stare at the road straight ahead", but scan instead of staring. Remember: Scan, never stare.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep your eyes moving: scan instead of staring, shifting your gaze constantly so you keep up with changing traffic.

question.text: How do you get the big picture?

answer.text: Get the big picture by keeping a proper following distance so you can judge the real hazards around your vehicle, and do not tailgate.

teaching.text: The aim high in steering rule says to aim high by looking far down the road, while the get the big picture rule says to get the big picture by keeping a proper following distance. Remember: Distance shows the hazards.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Get the big picture by keeping a proper following distance so you can judge the real hazards around your vehicle, and do not tailgate.

question.text: How do you leave yourself an out?

answer.text: Leave yourself an out by keeping open space in front of your vehicle and on at least one side so you can escape a conflict.

teaching.text: Asked "How do you leave yourself an out?" a tempting wrong answer is "Drive in the middle of a pack", but keep open space around you. Remember: Keep an escape space.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leave yourself an out by keeping open space in front of your vehicle and on at least one side so you can escape a conflict.

question.text: How do you make sure others see you?

answer.text: Make sure others see you by using your horn, lights and signals to make eye contact with drivers and pedestrians.

teaching.text: Asked "How can you make sure others see you?" a tempting wrong answer is "Drive faster than others", but use horn, lights and signals. Remember: Horn, lights, eye contact.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Make sure others see you by using your horn, lights and signals to make eye contact with drivers and pedestrians.

question.text: What should you know before acting on others' intentions?

answer.text: Be reasonably sure of other people's intentions before you act on them.

teaching.text: Asked "Before acting on what you think another road user will do, what should you be?" a tempting wrong answer is "In a hurry", but be reasonably sure first. Remember: Be reasonably sure.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Be reasonably sure of other people's intentions before you act on them.

question.text: What does defensive driving mean?

answer.text: Defensive driving means staying constantly aware of conditions, planning ahead, anticipating dangers and acting in time to avoid hitting any obstacle or vehicle.

teaching.text: Asked "Which best describes defensive driving?" a tempting wrong answer is "Driving as fast as traffic allows", but it means staying aware and acting in time. Remember: Aware, plan, act early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Defensive driving means staying constantly aware of conditions, planning ahead, anticipating dangers and acting in time to avoid hitting any obstacle or vehicle.

question.text: What does a defensive driver expect from others?

answer.text: Driving defensively means expecting other people's errors and being ready to make up for them, while behaving predictably yourself so you do not confuse others.

teaching.text: Asked "A defensive driver expects other people to do what?" a tempting wrong answer is "Always follow the rules", but expect their errors. Remember: Expect errors, be predictable.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving defensively means expecting other people's errors and being ready to make up for them, while behaving predictably yourself so you do not confuse others.

question.text: Which attitudes does the manual call most important for safe driving?

answer.text: The manual calls courtesy and consideration toward others the most important driving attitudes and the key to safe driving.

teaching.text: Asked "Which attitudes does the manual call the most important for safe driving?" a tempting wrong answer is "Speed and confidence", but courtesy and consideration. Remember: Courtesy is key.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The manual calls courtesy and consideration toward others the most important driving attitudes and the key to safe driving.

question.text: What can even a no-injury collision cost you?

answer.text: Even a collision with no injuries brings inconvenience and repair bills and can lead to court, fines and higher insurance rates, so a clean record protects you financially.

teaching.text: Asked "What can even a collision with no injuries bring?" a tempting wrong answer is "Nothing", but repair bills, fines and higher rates. Remember: Clean record saves money.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Even a collision with no injuries brings inconvenience and repair bills and can lead to court, fines and higher insurance rates, so a clean record protects you financially.

question.text: What should you expect another driver to do?

answer.text: Expect the other driver to do the wrong thing, and have a plan ready to counter the mistake.

teaching.text: Asked "What should you expect the other driver to do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Always the right thing", but expect the wrong thing. Remember: Plan for mistakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Expect the other driver to do the wrong thing, and have a plan ready to counter the mistake.

question.text: How much road information comes through your eyes?

answer.text: Drivers take in about ninety percent of their information about the road and surroundings through their eyes.

teaching.text: Asked "About how much of a driver's road information comes through the eyes?" a tempting wrong answer is "About ten percent", but about ninety percent. Remember: Eyes do most work.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drivers take in about ninety percent of their information about the road and surroundings through their eyes.

question.text: Why is concentration so important behind the wheel?

answer.text: Concentration is one of the most important parts of safe driving, so daydreaming, sightseeing and distracting conversations have no place behind the wheel.

teaching.text: Asked "Why have daydreaming and sightseeing no place behind the wheel?" a tempting wrong answer is "They waste fuel", but they break concentration. Remember: No daydreaming at the wheel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Concentration is one of the most important parts of safe driving, so daydreaming, sightseeing and distracting conversations have no place behind the wheel.

question.text: How far ahead should a defensive driver focus?

answer.text: Defensive drivers focus their eyes about ten to fifteen seconds ahead, roughly one city block, so they see trouble early and have more time to react.

teaching.text: The ten to fifteen seconds ahead rule keeps your eyes ten to fifteen seconds ahead, while the mirror every ten seconds rule has you check the mirror about every ten seconds. Remember: About a city block.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Defensive drivers focus their eyes about ten to fifteen seconds ahead, roughly one city block, so they see trouble early and have more time to react.

question.text: Which clues show a vehicle may pull into your path?

answer.text: Watch for exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights and turned wheels, which signal that a vehicle may pull into your path.

teaching.text: Asked "Which clue signals that a parked vehicle may pull into your path?" a tempting wrong answer is "A clean windshield", but exhaust smoke, lights or turned wheels. Remember: Smoke, lights, wheels.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch for exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights and turned wheels, which signal that a vehicle may pull into your path.

question.text: What should you scan for from side to side?

answer.text: Scan from side to side for directional signs and for cars or people that could be in the road by the time you get there.

teaching.text: The scan side to side rule says to scan side to side for signs and people, while the rural hazards rule lists rural hazards such as hidden driveways and gravel. Remember: Signs, cars and people.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Scan from side to side for directional signs and for cars or people that could be in the road by the time you get there.

question.text: Which hazards should you watch for in rural areas?

answer.text: In rural areas, watch for hidden intersections and driveways, curves, hills and changing road surfaces such as pavement turning to gravel or a narrowing road.

teaching.text: The scan side to side rule says to scan side to side for signs and people, while the rural hazards rule lists rural hazards such as hidden driveways and gravel. Remember: Hidden driveways, gravel, curves.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In rural areas, watch for hidden intersections and driveways, curves, hills and changing road surfaces such as pavement turning to gravel or a narrowing road.

question.text: In what order should you look before entering an intersection?

answer.text: Before entering any intersection, look left first because cars from the left are closer, then look right, then take one more quick look left.

teaching.text: The left, right, left rule tells you to look left, right, then left again before an intersection, and the clear the intersection rule says not to enter unless you can get all the way across. Remember: Left, right, left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before entering any intersection, look left first because cars from the left are closer, then look right, then take one more quick look left.

question.text: When must you check your rearview mirrors?

answer.text: Check your rearview mirrors constantly, and always check them before you change lanes.

teaching.text: Asked "When must you always check your rearview mirrors?" a tempting wrong answer is "Only when parking", but always before changing lanes. Remember: Mirrors before lane changes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check your rearview mirrors constantly, and always check them before you change lanes.

question.text: How often should you check your rearview mirror?

answer.text: Check your rearview mirror about every ten seconds to spot anyone closing too fast or tailgating, without taking your eyes off the road ahead for more than a brief glance.

teaching.text: The ten to fifteen seconds ahead rule keeps your eyes ten to fifteen seconds ahead, while the mirror every ten seconds rule has you check the mirror about every ten seconds. Remember: Mirror every ten seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check your rearview mirror about every ten seconds to spot anyone closing too fast or tailgating, without taking your eyes off the road ahead for more than a brief glance.

question.text: When should you look at the traffic behind you?

answer.text: Look at the traffic to your rear before a lane change, before backing, before braking hard and on long steep downgrades.

teaching.text: The when to look behind rule says when to look behind, and the mirror every ten seconds rule says how often to check the mirror. Remember: Look back before changes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Look at the traffic to your rear before a lane change, before backing, before braking hard and on long steep downgrades.

question.text: How does tracking traffic on every side help?

answer.text: When you track how fast and where the traffic is on every side of your car, you can decide quickly and safely in most situations.

teaching.text: Asked "What does tracking traffic on every side of your car let you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Drive faster", but decide quickly and safely. Remember: Know all sides.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you track how fast and where the traffic is on every side of your car, you can decide quickly and safely in most situations.

question.text: Why stay out of other drivers' blind spots?

answer.text: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots so that another vehicle does not turn into you.

teaching.text: Asked "Why stay out of other drivers' blind spots?" a tempting wrong answer is "To save fuel", but so a vehicle does not turn into you. Remember: Avoid blind spots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots so that another vehicle does not turn into you.

question.text: How does the two-second rule work?

answer.text: Follow the two-second rule: pick a fixed object ahead and count one thousand one, one thousand two; if you pass it before finishing, you are too close and should slow down.

teaching.text: The two-second rule sets two seconds as the normal following gap, while the three to four seconds rule raises it to at least three to four seconds on fast interstates, behind trucks or in bad weather. Remember: Count two seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Follow the two-second rule: pick a fixed object ahead and count one thousand one, one thousand two; if you pass it before finishing, you are too close and should slow down.

question.text: When should you increase your following gap to three or four seconds?

answer.text: On high-speed interstates, behind large trucks or buses, and in bad weather or poor visibility, increase your following gap to at least three to four seconds.

teaching.text: The two-second rule sets two seconds as the normal following gap, while the three to four seconds rule raises it to at least three to four seconds on fast interstates, behind trucks or in bad weather. Remember: More gap when risky.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On high-speed interstates, behind large trucks or buses, and in bad weather or poor visibility, increase your following gap to at least three to four seconds.

question.text: What causes rear-end crashes, and how much space prevents them?

answer.text: Rear-end crashes are very common and are caused by tailgating, so keep at least two seconds of space ahead, with extra room at railroad crossings and when stopped behind a vehicle on a hill or curve.

teaching.text: The rear-end crashes rule says tailgating causes rear-end crashes, and the steady speed, early signals rule says a steady speed and early signals keep a follower back. Remember: Two seconds, no tailgating.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rear-end crashes are very common and are caused by tailgating, so keep at least two seconds of space ahead, with extra room at railroad crossings and when stopped behind a vehicle on a hill or curve.

question.text: What is a safety cushion?

answer.text: Keep a safety cushion of space in front, behind and on each side of your vehicle so you have an escape route in an emergency.

teaching.text: Asked "Why keep a safety cushion of space on every side?" a tempting wrong answer is "To save fuel", but for an escape route. Remember: Space on every side.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep a safety cushion of space in front, behind and on each side of your vehicle so you have an escape route in an emergency.

question.text: What should you do when someone tailgates you?

answer.text: If someone tailgates you, move to the right lane if there is one; otherwise, once the way ahead is clear and a pass would be legal, ease off your speed gradually so the tailgater goes around.

teaching.text: The handling a tailgater rule says to move right or ease off so a tailgater goes around, while the never brake-check rule says never to brake suddenly at one. Remember: Move right or ease off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If someone tailgates you, move to the right lane if there is one; otherwise, once the way ahead is clear and a pass would be legal, ease off your speed gradually so the tailgater goes around.

question.text: Should you brake suddenly to discourage a tailgater?

answer.text: Never brake suddenly to discourage a tailgater, because it only raises your risk of being hit from behind.

teaching.text: The handling a tailgater rule says to move right or ease off so a tailgater goes around, while the never brake-check rule says never to brake suddenly at one. Remember: Never brake-check.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never brake suddenly to discourage a tailgater, because it only raises your risk of being hit from behind.

question.text: How can you keep a following driver at a safe distance?

answer.text: You can help keep a following driver at a safe distance by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down or turn.

teaching.text: The rear-end crashes rule says tailgating causes rear-end crashes, and the steady speed, early signals rule says a steady speed and early signals keep a follower back. Remember: Steady speed, signal early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You can help keep a following driver at a safe distance by holding a steady speed and signaling early before you slow down or turn.

question.text: What does communicating in traffic mean?

answer.text: Communicating in traffic means making your next move clear to drivers and pedestrians in time for them to avoid a collision.

teaching.text: Asked "What does communicating in traffic mean?" a tempting wrong answer is "Talking on the phone", but making your next move clear. Remember: Show your next move.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Communicating in traffic means making your next move clear to drivers and pedestrians in time for them to avoid a collision.

question.text: When should you use your turn signal?

answer.text: Use your turn signal any time you change direction, including lane changes, turns, entering an interstate and pulling to or from the curb, even when no other vehicle is in sight.

teaching.text: Asked "No other vehicle is in sight and you are pulling from the curb. Should you signal?" a tempting wrong answer is "No, only when others are near", but even when no one is in sight. Remember: Signal every direction change.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use your turn signal any time you change direction, including lane changes, turns, entering an interstate and pulling to or from the curb, even when no other vehicle is in sight.

question.text: How may you control the space around you?

answer.text: Controlling the space around you may mean slowing down or speeding up, but only within lawful limits.

teaching.text: Asked "When controlling the space around you, how may you change your speed?" a tempting wrong answer is "Exceed the limit if needed", but only within lawful limits. Remember: Adjust speed lawfully.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Controlling the space around you may mean slowing down or speeding up, but only within lawful limits.

question.text: Where should you ride when meeting oncoming traffic on a two-lane road?

answer.text: When meeting oncoming traffic on a two-lane road, keep a little right of center in your lane so you do not crowd the centerline.

teaching.text: Asked "Meeting oncoming traffic on a two-lane road, where should you keep your car?" a tempting wrong answer is "On the centerline", but keep a little right of center. Remember: A little right of center.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When meeting oncoming traffic on a two-lane road, keep a little right of center in your lane so you do not crowd the centerline.

question.text: How do you split the difference between two hazards?

answer.text: Split the difference between two hazards by steering a middle course, but give more room to the more dangerous one, such as an oncoming semi-truck rather than parked cars.

teaching.text: The split the difference rule steers a middle course between two hazards, while the one hazard at a time rule takes hazards one at a time. Remember: More room for bigger danger.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Split the difference between two hazards by steering a middle course, but give more room to the more dangerous one, such as an oncoming semi-truck rather than parked cars.

question.text: What should you do when a bicyclist and an oncoming car arrive together?

answer.text: Take hazards one at a time: when overtaking a bicyclist with an oncoming car approaching, slow down, let the car pass, then move left to give the bicycle room.

teaching.text: The split the difference rule steers a middle course between two hazards, while the one hazard at a time rule takes hazards one at a time. Remember: One hazard at a time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Take hazards one at a time: when overtaking a bicyclist with an oncoming car approaching, slow down, let the car pass, then move left to give the bicycle room.

question.text: Where should you leave extra space at the roadside?

answer.text: Leave extra space between your vehicle and parked cars, pedestrians and bicyclists at the roadside, especially children.

teaching.text: Asked "Whom should you especially give extra space at the roadside?" a tempting wrong answer is "Mailboxes", but especially children. Remember: Room for children especially.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leave extra space between your vehicle and parked cars, pedestrians and bicyclists at the roadside, especially children.

question.text: When is vision blocked enough to need extra space?

answer.text: Allow extra space when vision is blocked for you or another driver, for example by bushes at an intersection, glaring sun or pedestrians with umbrellas.

teaching.text: The blocked vision rule adds space when vision is blocked, while the distracted people rule adds space around distracted people. Remember: Blocked view, more space.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Allow extra space when vision is blocked for you or another driver, for example by bushes at an intersection, glaring sun or pedestrians with umbrellas.

question.text: Whom should you give extra space because they are distracted?

answer.text: Allow extra space around drivers or pedestrians who are distracted by phones, roadside attractions, sightseeing or tending to children.

teaching.text: The blocked vision rule adds space when vision is blocked, while the distracted people rule adds space around distracted people. Remember: Distracted people need room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Allow extra space around drivers or pedestrians who are distracted by phones, roadside attractions, sightseeing or tending to children.

question.text: How can you spot confused drivers or pedestrians?

answer.text: Allow extra space around confused drivers or pedestrians, such as those weaving between lanes, hunting for street names or reading maps.

teaching.text: Asked "A driver ahead weaves between lanes while hunting for street names. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Pass them closely", but allow extra space. Remember: Weaving or hunting means room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Allow extra space around confused drivers or pedestrians, such as those weaving between lanes, hunting for street names or reading maps.

question.text: How big a gap do you need to change lanes or merge?

answer.text: You need a gap of at least four seconds to change lanes, enter a roadway or merge, and you should cross several lanes one at a time, never cutting across them all at once.

teaching.text: The three to four seconds rule is the three to four second following gap, while the four-second merge gap rule is the four-second gap you need to change lanes or merge. Remember: Four seconds to merge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You need a gap of at least four seconds to change lanes, enter a roadway or merge, and you should cross several lanes one at a time, never cutting across them all at once.

question.text: What courtesy helps vehicles merging onto a multi-lane road?

answer.text: On multi-lane roads, be courteous and move to the left lane when other vehicles are trying to merge into traffic.

teaching.text: The make room for mergers rule asks you to move left for merging vehicles, while the sudden mergers rule asks you to slow down and leave room for sudden mergers. Remember: Move left for mergers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On multi-lane roads, be courteous and move to the left lane when other vehicles are trying to merge into traffic.

question.text: What can cutting across several lanes at once cause?

answer.text: Cutting across several lanes at once can tie up traffic, cause you to crash, or cause a crash between other drivers trying to avoid you.

teaching.text: The four-second merge gap rule says to cross several lanes one at a time, while the cutting across lanes rule warns that cutting across them all at once can cause a crash. Remember: Cutting across causes crashes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Cutting across several lanes at once can tie up traffic, cause you to crash, or cause a crash between other drivers trying to avoid you.

question.text: When may you enter an intersection?

answer.text: Do not enter an intersection unless you can get all the way across, and never block it or leave part of your vehicle in a lane of approaching traffic.

teaching.text: The left, right, left rule tells you to look left, right, then left again before an intersection, and the clear the intersection rule says not to enter unless you can get all the way across. Remember: Only if you can clear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not enter an intersection unless you can get all the way across, and never block it or leave part of your vehicle in a lane of approaching traffic.

question.text: How long a gap do you need to pass at fifty-five miles per hour?

answer.text: Passing at fifty-five miles per hour takes about ten seconds, so you need a ten-second gap in oncoming traffic and enough sight distance, and passing never allows you to exceed the speed limit.

teaching.text: The pass one at a time rule says to pass only one vehicle at a time, and the ten-second passing gap rule says a pass needs about a ten-second gap in oncoming traffic. Remember: Ten seconds to pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing at fifty-five miles per hour takes about ten seconds, so you need a ten-second gap in oncoming traffic and enough sight distance, and passing never allows you to exceed the speed limit.

question.text: When can you move back after passing?

answer.text: After passing, wait to move back into the driving lane until both headlights of the passed vehicle show in your rearview mirror.

teaching.text: The both headlights in the mirror rule says to return after passing once both headlights show in your mirror, and the room to return rule says not to count on the other driver to make room. Remember: Both headlights in mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After passing, wait to move back into the driving lane until both headlights of the passed vehicle show in your rearview mirror.

question.text: How many vehicles should you pass at one time?

answer.text: As a general rule, pass only one vehicle at a time, and do not pass unless there is room to return to the driving lane.

teaching.text: The pass one at a time rule says to pass only one vehicle at a time, and the ten-second passing gap rule says a pass needs about a ten-second gap in oncoming traffic. Remember: Pass one at a time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: As a general rule, pass only one vehicle at a time, and do not pass unless there is room to return to the driving lane.

question.text: Should you count on the passed driver to make room?

answer.text: When finishing a pass, do not count on the other driver to make room for you; you need enough space behind you to return safely.

teaching.text: The both headlights in the mirror rule says to return after passing once both headlights show in your mirror, and the room to return rule says not to count on the other driver to make room. Remember: Make your own room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When finishing a pass, do not count on the other driver to make room for you; you need enough space behind you to return safely.

question.text: What should you do when another driver passes without enough room?

answer.text: When another driver makes a mistake, such as passing without enough room, do not make it worse; slow down and give that driver room to get back into the lane.

teaching.text: Asked "A driver ahead passes without enough room and needs to get back into the lane. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Speed up to block them", but slow down and give room. Remember: Give them room back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When another driver makes a mistake, such as passing without enough room, do not make it worse; slow down and give that driver room to get back into the lane.

question.text: When should you slow down for drivers merging suddenly?

answer.text: Slow down and leave room for drivers merging suddenly around road hazards, from ending lanes, or onto and off expressways.

teaching.text: The make room for mergers rule asks you to move left for merging vehicles, while the sudden mergers rule asks you to slow down and leave room for sudden mergers. Remember: Room for sudden mergers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down and leave room for drivers merging suddenly around road hazards, from ending lanes, or onto and off expressways.

question.text: What can force another driver into your lane?

answer.text: Slow down and leave room for drivers who may be forced into your lane by another merging vehicle, road construction or emergency vehicles on the roadside.

teaching.text: The sudden mergers rule covers drivers merging suddenly around hazards or from ending lanes, while the drivers forced into your lane rule covers drivers forced into your lane by others. Remember: Forced mergers need room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down and leave room for drivers who may be forced into your lane by another merging vehicle, road construction or emergency vehicles on the roadside.

question.text: What share of traffic deaths does the manual tie to aggressive driving?

answer.text: The manual cites the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration as saying about sixty-six percent of yearly traffic deaths are caused by aggressive driving such as passing on the right, running red lights and tailgating.

teaching.text: Asked "According to the agency the manual cites, about what share of yearly traffic deaths are caused by aggressive driving?" a tempting wrong answer is "About six percent", but about sixty-six percent. Remember: Aggression kills most.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The manual cites the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration as saying about sixty-six percent of yearly traffic deaths are caused by aggressive driving such as passing on the right, running red lights and tailgating.

question.text: What counts as aggressive driving?

answer.text: Aggressive driving includes tailgating, honking, rude gestures, yelling, speeding, cutting others off and even using firearms.

teaching.text: The what aggressive driving is rule lists aggressive acts such as tailgating and honking, while the avoiding road rage rule says not to join a confrontation even by honking. Remember: Tailgating to firearms.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Aggressive driving includes tailgating, honking, rude gestures, yelling, speeding, cutting others off and even using firearms.

question.text: How are police and insurers treating aggressive drivers?

answer.text: Law enforcement agencies and insurance companies are getting much tougher on aggressive drivers.

teaching.text: Asked "How are law enforcement agencies and insurers treating aggressive drivers?" a tempting wrong answer is "They are easing up", but they are getting tougher. Remember: Getting tougher.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Law enforcement agencies and insurance companies are getting much tougher on aggressive drivers.

question.text: How do you avoid road rage?

answer.text: To avoid road rage, give driving your full attention, control your emotions and do not join a confrontation, even by honking or glaring.

teaching.text: The what aggressive driving is rule lists aggressive acts such as tailgating and honking, while the avoiding road rage rule says not to join a confrontation even by honking. Remember: Stay calm, do not engage.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To avoid road rage, give driving your full attention, control your emotions and do not join a confrontation, even by honking or glaring.

question.text: Which driving habits help you avoid road rage?

answer.text: To avoid road rage, obey the law, drive defensively, drive relaxed and within the speed limit, do not tailgate, and pass only when you need to.

teaching.text: Asked "Which habit helps you avoid road rage?" a tempting wrong answer is "Tailgating slow drivers", but do not tailgate. Remember: Relaxed, lawful, no tailgating.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To avoid road rage, obey the law, drive defensively, drive relaxed and within the speed limit, do not tailgate, and pass only when you need to.

question.text: How should you treat an angry driver?

answer.text: Give an angry driver plenty of space, and do not take traffic problems personally; stay polite even when others are rude.

teaching.text: Asked "How should you treat an angry driver near you?" a tempting wrong answer is "Stay close to show you are not scared", but give plenty of space. Remember: Give space, stay polite.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Give an angry driver plenty of space, and do not take traffic problems personally; stay polite even when others are rude.

question.text: What must a driver who gets angry behind the wheel do?

answer.text: A driver who tends to get angry behind the wheel must change that attitude and behavior, or becomes a crash waiting to happen.

teaching.text: Asked "A driver tends to get angry behind the wheel. What must that driver do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Drive faster to vent", but change the attitude. Remember: Change the angry attitude.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver who tends to get angry behind the wheel must change that attitude and behavior, or becomes a crash waiting to happen.

question.text: What should you do if another driver follows you?

answer.text: If a driver follows you, go to a police station or another public place where you can get help.

teaching.text: The if you are followed rule says to drive to a police station if a driver follows you, while the if you are harassed rule says to get the plate number and report a driver who harasses you. Remember: Go to a police station.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a driver follows you, go to a police station or another public place where you can get help.

question.text: What should you do if you are harassed on the road?

answer.text: If you are harassed on the road, try to get the offender's license plate number and report the incident to the authorities.

teaching.text: The if you are followed rule says to drive to a police station if a driver follows you, while the if you are harassed rule says to get the plate number and report a driver who harasses you. Remember: Get the plate, report.
